The rain didn’t fall; it hammered. It struck the glass of the lantern room with the rhythmic violence of a thousand tiny fists, blurring the horizon into a smear of charcoal and slate. Elias Thorne wiped the condensation from the lens, his breath pluming in the sudden chill that had nothing to do with the weather. He was seventy-two, his knuckles swollen like knotted rope, and he had kept the light at Cape Dusk for forty years. He knew the sea’s moods better than he knew his own daughter’s.

The radio crackled. It wasn’t the static of the storm, nor the usual chatter of the fishing trawlers. It was a clear, high-pitched tone, followed by a voice that sounded like it was being pulled through a vacuum.

"Keeper Thorne. Do not extinguish the lamp. Do not leave the room. The coordinates are wrong. The ship is not where you think it is."

Elias froze, his hand hovering over the emergency cutoff switch. "Who is this? This is a private frequency."
